PART 1: NARRATION READY
What you are looking at with DELIF is a transformer that is working significantly harder than it needs to — and paying a measurable price for it every single day. Across all of May, your average power factor on this transformer sat at 85.26 percent. That means for every hundred units of electrical capacity moving through this transformer, roughly fifteen of them are circulating reactive current — spinning through motors, cycling compressors, sustaining inductive loads — without producing a single watt of useful output. At an average draw of 770 kVA and a peak demand pushing 1,544 kVA — which is also your supply ceiling — you are running this transformer close to its limit during production hours with a significant reactive penalty baked in. The voltage field confirms the stress. Your average voltage sits right at nominal — 277.77 volts line-to-neutral — but the operating band tells the real story. You are seeing sags down to 456.9 volts line-to-line during inductive load events. That is nearly 5 percent below nominal, and in a food processing environment those sags accumulate insulation stress on every motor winding, every drive, every control system that experiences them. And the data confirms at least one complete field collapse during the month — a zero-volt event lasting an estimated 60 to 90 minutes near the end of May. The reactive draw is averaging 347.7 kVAR with a planning-basis maximum of 556 kVAR. The thermal burden from all of this reactive cycling is sitting at 323,371 BTU per hour — heat that costs roughly $82,759 per year just to manage. Total estimated annual waste is approximately $248,000. With two H490 units correcting this field to 99.5 percent power factor, that waste largely disappears. The planning investment estimate is approximately $400,000 installed. That is the correction this field needs. ---

PART 2: EXECUTIVE SHORT
The DELIF transformer is running at 85.26 percent average power factor across May — meaning about 15 percent of its capacity is tied up circulating reactive current that does no real work. Peak demand reaches 1,544 kVA, which is the supply ceiling, so the transformer is regularly at its limit during production windows. Voltage quality is a concern — sags to 456.9 volts line-to-line are recurring during production, and there was one confirmed field collapse of approximately 60 to 90 minutes near month-end. The thermal burden is 323,371 BTU per hour, with cooling costs running roughly $82,759 per year. Total annual waste is estimated at approximately $248,000. MPTS correction brings power factor to 99.5 percent. Two H490 units are sized for this transformer. Planning-level investment is approximately $400,000 installed. The waste recovery offsets that investment while also improving voltage stability and reducing thermal stress on equipment that is currently operating under chronic reactive burden. That's electromagnetic stewardship — and that's the Unity standard. --- Pricing note: these figures are planning-level estimates, not final quotes. Final installed pricing depends on engineering scope, labor, and site conditions. For planning, estimated installed investment is roughly $340,000 to $460,000.

PART 3: ENGINEERING DETAILED
Let me walk you through the DELIF transformer field in full detail, because this is a transformer where every layer of the data reinforces the same conclusion — this field needs reactive compensation, and it needs it now. Start with the foundation. Forty-four thousand six hundred forty minutes of one-minute-resolution capture across May 2026. That is thirty-one full days of continuous field observation. The CSV ground truth gives us an average power factor of 85.26 percent. That number sounds reasonable in isolation, but consider what it means operationally. At an average apparent demand of 770.2 kVA, your actual useful power output is 683.5 kilowatts. The difference — the reactive component — is averaging 347.7 kVAR every minute of every production hour. That reactive current is not doing work. It is circulating. It is heating conductors. It is stressing insulation. It is loading your transformer beyond what your real production load alone would require. Now look at the peak demand picture. Your P95 kVA — the demand level you are at or below 95 percent of the time — is 1,543.9 kVA. And that is also your supply target, your daily ceiling. So by definition, 5 percent of your operating time, you are pushing above that ceiling. The BT view confirms this visually — weekday production columns are regularly exceeding the 1,544 kVA target line. In an untuned, reactive-heavy field, operating at or above the supply ceiling accelerates transformer aging and reduces protection headroom. The voltage picture deepens the concern. Your mean voltage is essentially at nominal — 277.77 volts line-to-neutral, which is 480.8 volts line-to-line. Perfect average, troubled reality. The V-view shows a persistently oscillating trace with triangular sag events clustering during production windows. The worst annotated sag reaches 456.9 volts line-to-line — a 4.8 percent drop below nominal. In a facility running refrigeration compressors, processing motors, conveyor systems, and sensitive drive electronics simultaneously, a 4.8 percent sag is not a nuisance event. It is a reliability stressor that accumulates with every occurrence. Motor windings run hotter during under-voltage conditions. Drive electronics stress their voltage conversion circuits. Control systems can trip on nuisance faults. And then there is the zero-volt event. The image confirms a gold vertical streak running the full height of the BT chart body near the May 29 to 30 date range — one confirmed site power-off interval of approximately 60 to 90 minutes. A full field collapse. Whether that was a planned shutdown, an upstream fault, or a protection trip driven by field stress is a question worth answering. What we know is that it happened, and it happened in a transformer field that was already under significant reactive and thermal burden. The reactive picture from the M-view makes the thermal story concrete. Peak current hits 1,865.4 amps — roughly double the running average of 928.1 amps. That is the inductive surge signature of large motors starting, compressors cycling on, heavy equipment engaging. During those events, the power factor drops to as low as 72.58 percent. At 72.58 percent, nearly 28 percent of the apparent power is reactive waste. The harmonic contamination layer — averaging 5.2 percent iTHD with peaks to 10.4 percent — sits persistently at the base of the M-view throughout the month. Harmonics add heating in the transformer windings above and beyond the fundamental-frequency reactive losses. Combined with a reactive surge profile this intense, the result is a thermal burden of 323,371 BTU per hour — and roughly $82,759 per year in cooling costs just to keep the equipment from overheating. Total estimated annual waste — reactive losses plus thermal burden plus cooling overhead — runs to approximately $248,000 per year by the image-based analysis. Every month this field runs untuned, that waste accumulates. The MPTS simulation shows the corrected state clearly. Two H490 units, sized from the CSV-anchored planning kVAR maximum of 556 kVAR, bring this field to 99.5 percent power factor. The reactive current that currently averages 347.7 kVAR is supplied locally by the MPTS units at the load — it never travels upstream through the transformer, the conductors, or the supply infrastructure. Current drops on the supply path. Conductor losses drop. Transformer winding heating drops. Voltage stability improves because the reactive surge currents that are currently creating those triangular sag events are being damped at source. The planning-level investment for two H490 units is approximately $400,000 installed — with final pricing dependent on engineering scope and site

Discrete triangular voltage-drop events are clearly visible and they cluster during active production windows. The annotated minimum dip reaches 456.9 volts line-to-line — approximately 23 volts below the 480-volt nominal, representing a 4.8 percent sag. The image header records a confirmed minimum of 0.0 volts — indicating at least one complete voltage collapse during the month. This corresponds to the outage event identified in the BT view: one gold vertical streak detected near the 260529 to 260530 date range, estimated at approximately 60 to 90 minutes of site power-off duration. This is not a momentary motor-induced sag. This is a full-field interruption.

The voltage spread from the operating minimum dip of 456.9 volts to the upper swell of 497.7 volts represents a range of approximately 41 volts across the month. That is a wide operating envelope for equipment rated to tight voltage tolerances. The device health implication is assessed as high risk — recurring sub-nominal dips combined with a confirmed zero-volt collapse event put motor windings, drive electronics, and control system components under chronic cumulative stress.

**DELIF Transformer — Reactive and Harmonic Findings | May 2026**

The M-view — the Active-Reactive view for DELIF in May 2026 — delivers the clearest single picture of why this field is operating so inefficiently. The reactive current story is not subtle. It is dominant, persistent, and violent during surge events.

The CSV ground truth anchors the average reactive draw at 347.7 kVAR across all 44,640 minutes of capture. That is not a peak — that is the floor. The field never relaxes below a substantial reactive current draw during production hours because the inductive load base — motors, compressors, refrigeration systems — requires continuous magnetizing current. The planning-basis kVAR MAX used for MPTS sizing is 556 kVAR, derived from the CSV P95 profile. The image header records a transient peak of 1,150 kVAR during the most intense surge events — a reminder that instantaneous reactive demand during large motor starts can spike far above the sustained average.

Peak amperage in the M-view reaches 1,865.4 amps against a running average of 928.1 amps. That is nearly double the average current occurring during surge events — a severe inductive surge profile that represents real mechanical and thermal stress on transformer windings, bus connections, and protective devices.

The power factor story compounds the reactive picture. The CSV-confirmed average is 85.26 percent, and that already signals meaningful inefficiency. But the M-view image reveals the true operational range: the minimum power factor dips to 72.58 percent during surge events. At 72.58 percent, nearly 28 percent of the apparent power flowing through this transformer is doing no useful work whatsoever. For a transformer processing nearly 800 kVA on average and peaking well above 1,500 kVA, that represents a substantial volume of wasted electrical energy.

The harmonic picture adds a compounding stress layer. The image confirms 5.2 percent iTHD average with a 10.4 percent maximum — a persistent harmonic contamination floor that never reaches zero during production. Sustained harmonics at these levels generate additional winding heating beyond the fundamental-frequency reactive losses, accelerating insulation aging and contributing to the 323,371 BTU per hour thermal burden reported in the BT header. The combination of high reactive surge current and continuous harmonic contamination is one of the most thermally corrosive pairings a transformer can experience in continuous operation.

This is the nature of an untuned field — it does not hold steady. It drifts. Equipment ages, insulation degrades, and the reactive burden tends to rise as motors and compressors accumulate wear and their power factor characteristics worsen.

The thermal burden quantifies what the reactive and harmonic losses cost in physical terms. The BT header reports 323,371 BTU per hour of thermal load on the transformer and associated equipment. When a transformer routinely operates at or above its supply ceiling in an untuned, reactive-heavy field, the cumulative effect is accelerated aging of insulation systems, elevated risk of thermal protection trips, and reduced headroom for load growth or process expansion.

The one confirmed outage event — approximately 60 to 90 minutes near the end of May — may or may not be operationally connected to field stress. But it is noted: a transformer operating under sustained reactive burden and voltage turbulence is statistically more vulnerable to protection events than one operating in a clean, corrected field. The untuned condition is not a background nuisance. It is an active contributor to reliability risk.

Without MPTS correction assigned to this transformer, the field continues to waste roughly $153,543 per year in energy losses, with total waste estimated at approximately $248,128 annually when thermal and cooling overhead are included. Every month of delay is a month of that cost accumulating without return.

The following areas warrant priority engineering attention for the DELIF transformer based on the May 2026 field analysis.

**Reactive compensation — MPTS sizing and placement:** Two H490 units are indicated based on the 556 kVAR planning maximum. Engineering site assessment should confirm optimal placement relative to the dominant inductive load centers — refrigeration compressor banks and processing line motor groups are the likely primary targets. Placement at load rather than at the transformer bus maximizes reactive current path reduction.

**Voltage quality investigation:** The confirmed 0.0-volt minimum and the recurring 456.9-volt sag events warrant a dedicated power quality investigation to identify whether the protection event near month-end is related to field stress, upstream supply, or a specific load switching sequence. Variable frequency drives and switching power supplies in the load mix are likely harmonic contributors, and MPTS correction alone does not eliminate harmonic distortion.

**Thermal management review:** At 323,371 BTU per hour of thermal burden, the transformer and surrounding electrical infrastructure should be assessed for cooling adequacy, particularly during summer months when ambient temperatures in the Central Valley will compound the thermal stress significantly. The $82,759 annual cooling cost estimate underscores the financial stakes of allowing this burden to persist.

**Load growth headroom:** With P95 demand already at the 1,544 kVA supply ceiling, any planned production expansion requires reactive correction first — otherwise load growth pushes the transformer into sustained overload territory.
